message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"2.13","text":"For it is absolutely necessary that one who says God is just by nature should also believe that human souls are immortal. Otherwise, where is his justice, when some who lived devoutly, after sometimes being mistreated, were violently killed, while others who became exceedingly impious, after luxuriating in an affluent life, died the death common to human beings? Since, then, beyond all dispute God, being good, is also just, yet he will be recognized as just in no other way unless the soul is immortal after its separation from the body, so that the evil person, having come to Hades, may be punished there for the sins he committed, since he enjoyed good things here, while the good person, having been punished here for the sins he committed, may there be established as an heir to good things, as though in the bosoms of the just—therefore, since God is just, it is evident to us that judgment also takes place and that souls are indeed immortal.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα","chosen":"For it is absolutely necessary","rationale":"The idiom expresses complete necessity rather than a literal plurality of necessities."},{"source_quote":"τὸν κοινὸν ἀνθρώπων θάνατον ἐτελεύτησαν","chosen":"died the death common to human beings","rationale":"Preserves the claim that their deaths were ordinary human deaths, in contrast to the violent deaths just mentioned."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἐν κόλποις δικαίων","chosen":"as though in the bosoms of the just","rationale":"Retains the plural bodily image; δικαίων is understood substantivally as just people."},{"source_quote":"ὅτι τοίνυν ὁ θεὸς δίκαιος","chosen":"therefore, since God is just","rationale":"The first ὅτι is taken causally, while the following ὅτι introduces what is evident; taking the first as another content clause would leave the relationship between the clauses less clear."},{"source_quote":"ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι τυγχάνουσιν","chosen":"souls are indeed immortal","rationale":"τυγχάνω functions here with a predicate adjective; “prove to be immortal” is also possible but would place more emphasis on discovery."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.14","text":"But if anyone (as Simon the Samaritan thinks) is unwilling to grant God the attribute of being just, to whom else can anyone grant this, or even grant that it can come into being? For if the root of all things does not possess this, it is altogether necessary to understand that it is impossible to find it in human nature, as in the fruits. But if it can be found among human beings, how much more in God? And if justice can be found nowhere (neither with God nor with human beings), then assuredly neither can injustice. But justice does exist, for it is because justice exists that something is called unjust; just as it is called injustice when justice is placed beside it and found to stand in opposition.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ δικαίῳ εἶναι θεῷ","chosen":"God the attribute of being just","rationale":"The articular infinitival construction denotes the state or attribute of God’s being just."},{"source_quote":"ἢ καὶ τὸ γενέσθαι δύνασθαι","chosen":"or even grant that it can come into being","rationale":"The phrase is treated as a second object of the understood “grant.” An alternative is “or even grant the possibility of its coming into being.”"},{"source_quote":"τῆς ῥίζης τῶν ὅλων","chosen":"the root of all things","rationale":"Preserves the root-and-fruit analogy subsequently applied to God and human nature."},{"source_quote":"τὸ δίκαιον","chosen":"justice","rationale":"The substantivized adjective denotes what is just or justice as a quality; “what is just” is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ παραβαλλομένης τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτῇ καὶ ἐναντίως ἔχειν εὑρισκομένης ἀδικία λέγεται","chosen":"just as it is called injustice when justice is placed beside it and found to stand in opposition","rationale":"The repeated implicit referent of “it” is not fully explicit in the Greek. The rendering preserves that referential openness; alternatively, the final clause may be expressed as “what opposes justice is called injustice.”"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.15","text":"Hence, then, God, in teaching human beings about the truth of realities, though himself one, divided all the things at the extremes into two and as opposites. Being himself from the beginning the one and only God, he made heaven and earth, day and night, light and fire, sun and moon, life and death. But among these he made the human being alone self-determining, with the capacity to become just or unjust. For the human being he also reversed the patterns of the pairs, setting the first members before him as small and the second as great—for example, the world and the age. (For the present world is temporary, but the coming age is eternal.) Ignorance is first, knowledge second. Thus he also arranged the leaders of prophecy. For since the present world is female, like a mother of children giving birth to souls, while the coming age is male, like a father receiving his own children, prophets accordingly come into this world as sons of the coming age, possessing knowledge of human beings. If people who live in reverence for God had understood this mystery, they would never have gone astray, but even now would have recognized that Simon, who is now throwing everyone into confusion, is a collaborator of the weak left side. The account of the prophetic rule runs as follows:","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὄντων ἀλήθειαν","chosen":"about the truth of realities","rationale":"τὰ ὄντα denotes things that are or realities. The preposition may alternatively express purpose: “with a view to the truth of realities.”"},{"source_quote":"διχῶς καὶ ἐναντίως διεῖλεν πάντα τὰ τῶν ἄκρων","chosen":"divided all the things at the extremes into two and as opposites","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the twofold division and opposition without reducing τὰ τῶν ἄκρων to a specific list not stated in the phrase."},{"source_quote":"μόνον δὲ ἐν τούτοις αὐτεξούσιον τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐποίησεν","chosen":"But among these he made the human being alone self-determining","rationale":"μόνον is taken with “the human being,” making humanity alone αὐτεξούσιος among the listed creations. A less likely attachment is “only in these matters he made the human being self-determining.”"},{"source_quote":"τὰς τῶν συζυγιῶν ἐνήλλαξεν εἰκόνας","chosen":"reversed the patterns of the pairs","rationale":"εἰκόνας literally means “images,” while “patterns” conveys the ordered correspondences; ἐνήλλαξεν indicates reversal or interchange."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς τῆς προφητείας ἡγεμόνας διέταξεν","chosen":"arranged the leaders of prophecy","rationale":"The context concerns ordering paired figures. “Appointed the leaders of prophecy” is also grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"ἀνθρώπων τὴν γνῶσιν ἔχοντες","chosen":"possessing knowledge of human beings","rationale":"The genitive is taken objectively. It could instead mean “possessing human knowledge” or “possessing the knowledge belonging to human beings.”"},{"source_quote":"τῆς ἀσθενοῦς ἀριστερᾶς","chosen":"of the weak left side","rationale":"ἀριστερά may denote the left hand or the left side; “side” fits the preceding scheme of opposed pairs while retaining the spatial image."},{"source_quote":"ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ προφητικοῦ κανόνος οὕτως ἔχει","chosen":"The account of the prophetic rule runs as follows","rationale":"λόγος is rendered “account” as the formulation that follows; “principle” or “reasoning” would also be possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"2.16","text":"Just as in the beginning God, being one, first made heaven, like the right hand, and then earth, like the left, and in this way constituted all the pairs in succession, with human beings, however, it is no longer this way; instead, he reverses all the pairs. For while the first things from him are better and the second inferior, among human beings we find the opposite: the first inferior and the second better. Thus, to begin with, from Adam, who came into being according to God’s image, there arose someone who was first and unjust, Cain, and a second who was just, Abel. Again, from the one you call Deucalion, two images of spirits were sent out—I mean of an unclean spirit and a clean one: the black raven and, second, the white dove. From Abraham, the founder of our nation, the first two arose: first Ishmael, then Isaac, who was blessed by God. And from Isaac himself, likewise, again two arose: the impious Esau and the devout Jacob. Thus, in order, first—as firstborn for the world—is the high priest, and then the lawgiver.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ δεξιὰ καὶ ἀριστερά","chosen":"like the right hand ... like the left","rationale":"The adjectives are substantivized and may mean the right and left hand or side; “hand” preserves the familiar paired bodily image."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ μέντοι ἀνθρώπων","chosen":"with human beings, however","rationale":"ἐπί marks the sphere or case in which the ordering is reversed, not necessarily physical location."},{"source_quote":"ὡς γὰρ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τὰ πρῶτα κρείττονα, τὰ δεύτερα ἥττονα","chosen":"For while the first things from him are better and the second inferior","rationale":"The elliptical clause is supplied with an English copula. “Since the first things from him are better” is an alternative treatment of ὡς."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς λεγομένου Δευκαλίωνος","chosen":"the one you call Deucalion","rationale":"καθ’ ὑμᾶς marks the addressees’ naming or tradition rather than identifying Deucalion as the author’s own conventional name."},{"source_quote":"πνευμάτων εἰκόνες δύο","chosen":"two images of spirits","rationale":"Retains the explicit characterization of the raven and dove as representations of two kinds of spirit."},{"source_quote":"δύο πρῶτοι γεγόνασιν","chosen":"the first two arose","rationale":"The phrase is compressed and lacks an expressed noun such as “sons” or “offspring.” The rendering preserves the ordinal language without inserting that noun."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πρωτότοκος τῷ κόσμῳ","chosen":"as firstborn for the world","rationale":"The dative can express relation or perspective. Alternatives include “as firstborn in the world” and “as firstborn from the world’s standpoint.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"(ὡς γὰρ","issue":"The supplied passage contains an opening parenthesis before this phrase but no matching closing parenthesis within section 2.16. The parenthetical scope may continue beyond the supplied excerpt, so this is an editorial-punctuation uncertainty rather than an unreadable construction. The translation uses ordinary sentence punctuation without assigning a conjectural closing point.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
